props.title: The Rain People
props.initialSlug: Housewife flees family, finds troubled souls on the road

sections.content: **The Rain People (1969)** (1969) marks a pivotal moment in Francis Ford Coppola's early career, bridging his student films and his later masterpieces like **The Godfather** (1972). This haunting road movie follows Natalie Ravenna, a housewife who discovers she's pregnant and flees her suburban life, picking up a brain-damaged ex-football player named Killer along the way. Shot guerrilla-style with a small crew traveling across America, it shares DNA with contemporary New Hollywood classics like **Easy Rider** (1969) and Five Easy Pieces (1970) in its exploration of alienation and escape from conventional society.

sections.content: Coppola's innovative production methods on **The Rain People** (1969) proved influential, with George Lucas documenting the shoot for his behind-the-scenes film **Filmmaker** (1968). The mobile filmmaking unit they developed would later inspire the independent production approach of **American Graffiti** (1973) and **Mean Streets** (1973). Shirley Knight's raw performance as Natalie predates similar character studies like **Alice Doesn't Live Here Anymore** (1974) and **A Woman Under the Influence** (1974).

The film's exploration of damaged masculinity through James Caan's character Killer connects to later New Hollywood examinations of male vulnerability like **The Last Detail** (1973) and **Midnight Cowboy** (1969). Robert Duvall's portrayal of the controlling highway patrolman Gordon also foreshadows his later collaborations with Coppola, particularly in **The Godfather** (1972) and **Apocalypse Now** (1979). SUBHEAD: New Hollywood's Road Movie Revolution

sections.content: **The Rain People** (1969) emerged during a crucial shift in American cinema when the road movie became a vessel for examining national identity and social upheaval. While **Bonnie and Clyde** (1967) had established the outlaw couple template, Coppola's film shares more with introspective journeys like **Scarecrow** (1973) and **Alice Doesn't Live Here Anymore** (1974), where the physical journey mirrors internal transformation.
